arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE RECORD DOES NOT REACH THE DAY. Every source that names this person falls on one side of 1 July 1835, and nothing follows them to it or says they left. `uncertain` rather than dropped — the distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and a finding, not a gap. AND THE BRACKET THIS CARD ONCE HAD IS WITHDRAWN, NOT LOST: its at-or-before leg was tax_1833 alone. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago, so it cannot say this person was here to be followed across the day. Withdrawn to `uncertain` and not to `absent` — no source places this person anywhere else on 1 July 1835 either, and a man who was taxed for ground in the town may perfectly well have been standing on it.

dated_bounds.note: PROPERTY, NOT PRESENCE (T-1117). Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 names the owners of ground inside the town, resident or not — its entry 110 is Alexander Wolcott, who had been dead since 25 October 1830 — so this row bounds what this person was assessed for and says nothing about where the person was. tools/assert_tax_roll_ruling.py holds that ruling on the two readings it rests on. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT. The reading of the roll is documented — the town's own paper, held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository, twice mediated by Schulz's transcription and Genealogy Trails' republication, which this project has not gone behind. What no source states is that the man on the roll is the person on this card: data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json joins them on a name, by its rule “one resident of the surname 'Morrison' agrees with the entry's forenames; 5 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.”, and forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Orsemus Morrison' against resident 'Orsemus Morrison'. A bound whose subject is inferred is an inferred bound. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Morrison, Orsemus” (tax_1833_076, line 128). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Morrison' agrees with the entry's forenames; 5 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

merge_ruling.for_merge: The surname agrees letter for letter, d and s are one substitution apart in a worn impression, and Orsemus Morrison is one of the town's documented carpenters: the 1833 tax list, Fergus 1843 ('Morrison, Orsemus, carpenter, res 153 Clark [died Jan. 4,1864, a. 58½]') and Norris 1844 ('carpenter, house Clark st'). 'Ordemus' is a forename that exists nowhere else in the corpus, which is the profile of a mis-read rather than a man.
merge_ruling.against_merge: TWO ROLLS OF ONE TRANSCRIPTION, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'Morrison, Orsemus' is the 1833 tax list (line 128) and 'Morrison, Ordemus' the poll filed 11 August 1834 (line 245) — and that poll also enters 'Morrison, J. M.' at line 244, so the roll that set Ordemus was setting Morrisons carefully. No roll sets both forenames; a shared source id is not a shared printing. The town holds five Morrison cards, so the surname decides nothing. D9, and the forename's absence from the rest of the corpus is kept in `for_merge` because it is what a reading of the 1834 poll's image would test.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('morrison_orsemus:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a poll, tax or muster list names a person 20 or over - the 1840 schedule's own adult line. THE FRANCHISE'S AGE RULE IS NOT IN ANY SOURCE RECORD THIS PROJECT HOLDS; this is the model's conditioning and not a reading (T-1303's finding, handed to T-1304). No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
